packet.evidence_limit: Review covers the submitted passage and its editing rationale. Several voices and arrangements can serve the same reader. Whether real readers understood it needs a reader observation. Fiction, poetry, the learner's overall talent and any private writing remain outside this finding.
packet.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer
packet.learner: Can we try two versions of the lamp notice, one with the line about volunteers and one without? I want to see which is easier to scan.

material.excerpt: A new reader may see two possible actions. Look for the detail that tells them which applies. Trace each path through the draft before deciding whether the wording will do.
material.lesson: For a passage with two possible actions, imagine the reader encountering each situation separately. Read only what you have put on the page. See whether either reader has to supply a missing rule.

packet.new_task: Write a short onboarding note for a new library volunteer shelving returns. Items with a blue dot stay on the cart for staff to check. Unmarked items go on the shelves. The draft says, 'Put the returns where they belong.' Revise it in your own voice and explain one edit that helps the new volunteer decide what to do.
packet.policy: Resume the goal on a different task using the available history.

receipt.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer

response.display:
Let’s try that with the library returns note.

**With the volunteer line**
New volunteers, here’s how to sort returns.
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

**Without the volunteer line**
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

Scan each version once for a blue-dot return and once for an unmarked return. Which version helps you find both actions faster? Then write your own version and explain one edit that helps a new volunteer decide where a return goes.
